column4: The command قُومُوا۟ لِلَّهِ مَثْنَىٰ وَفُرَٰدَىٰ places people explicitly “in pairs and singly,” turning the section’s abstract even/odd opposition into a human posture of reflection.
This ayah holds both sides of the section together: creatures receive أَزْوَٰجًا, while لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِۦ شَىْءٌ denies any counterpart to their Creator.
People come to God فُرَٰدَىٰ as first created, and the presumed شُفَعَاء are absent; the ayah itself joins the section’s solitary return to the failure of hoped-for supporters.

رَضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ states the two-way pleasure developed in the section, then names those people حِزْبُ ٱللَّهِ, matching its gloss of entering God’s servants as entering His party.
God is pleased with them and they with Him, and gardens follow; this makes the paired رضى relation the condition of the same communal garden-ending heard in 89:28-30.
On the day when truthfulness benefits the truthful, رَضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ makes the section’s two-sided satisfaction explicit and associates it with entry into gardens.
The mutual formula رَّضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ is attached to a named community and prepared gardens, expanding the lone soul’s acceptance into an accepted company.
Humankind and jinn cannot bring بِمِثْلِ هَٰذَا ٱلْقُرْءَانِ even if they become supporters of one another; unmatched likeness and collective backing meet in one claim.
Human plurality begins from نَّفْسٍ وَٰحِدَةٍ, receives its mate, and spreads into many men and women; it is the section’s movement from one, to pair, to community in a single creation scene.
ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ gives true oneness to God, directly grounding the section’s distinction between a remarkable created singleton and the One without ontological peer.
وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُۥ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ denies every equivalent to God, supplying the precise boundary behind the section’s language of an unmatched counterpart.
وَمِن كُلِّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَا زَوْجَيْنِ states the created order as pairs and makes remembering the Creator the intended inference.
Every creature comes to God on resurrection فَرْدًا, making the section’s unaccompanied “one” an eschatological condition rather than an abstract number.
A good or bad شَفَاعَة gives its maker a corresponding share, showing the source root’s social sense as deliberately joining a cause in support rather than merely forming a numerical pair.
The command to improve the orphans’ condition culminates in وَإِن تُخَالِطُوهُمْ فَإِخْوَٰنُكُمْ; mixing with them as brothers is the clearest Quranic enactment of not leaving the orphan single.
Solomon asks God to أَدْخِلْنِى ... فِى عِبَادِكَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ, nearly restaging the section’s singular addressee being admitted among God’s servants.
يَٰعِبَادِ directly addresses God’s servants on the last day with freedom from fear and grief; 43:69-70 identifies them and completes their communal entry into the Garden.
This ayah identifies the servants addressed in 43:68 as believers who submitted, giving the group into which the final Garden command of 43:70 admits them.
ٱدْخُلُوا۟ ٱلْجَنَّةَ أَنتُمْ وَأَزْوَٰجُكُمْ commands the servants to enter the Garden with their spouses, combining communal entry and pairing in the closest parallel to 89:29-30.
ثَانِىَ ٱثْنَيْنِ stages two companions under threat, while “God is with us” prevents the vulnerable second from being alone; number becomes loyal accompaniment.
Two messengers are sent and then strengthened with a third, فَعَزَّزْنَا بِثَالِثٍ; addition here is explicitly the addition of support, matching the section’s social definition of joining another.
No private group of three, five, fewer, or more lacks God’s presence with them; the numbered sequence makes divine accompaniment the answer to apparent human solitude.
Intercession benefits only with the Merciful’s permission and approved speech, linking شفاعة to رضى and placing a divine boundary around who may stand beside another.
وَلَا يَشْفَعُونَ إِلَّا لِمَنِ ٱرْتَضَىٰ joins the section’s two roots in one rule: intercessors support only someone God has approved.
Even many angels’ شَفَاعَة is useless until God permits it for one He wills and approves; multitude alone cannot overcome the solitary judgment described in the section.
On the warned-of day no soul avails another, no شَفَاعَة is accepted, and no help arrives; every form of standing beside someone is removed together.
No soul can compensate for another and no intercession benefits it, directly staging the judgment-day limit of the section’s “joining as supporter and asker.”
Before the day with neither bargaining, friendship, nor شَفَاعَة, giving is urged; present solidarity must occur before those relationships can no longer be used.
مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُۥٓ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِۦ makes permission the exact boundary: an intercessor can join another’s case only under God’s authority.
Those fearing assembly before their Lord are warned that they have no protector or شَفِيع besides Him, sharpening the section’s image of the person without an attached supporter.
A soul held for what it earned has neither protector nor شَفِيع and cannot ransom itself, so social and material additions both fail at judgment.
Those facing the fulfilled warning ask whether any شُفَعَاء can intercede or whether they can return; their request exposes too late the support they lack.
مَا مِن شَفِيعٍ إِلَّا مِنۢ بَعْدِ إِذْنِهِ makes God’s permission the boundary to all intercessory joining.
The worshippers call other beings “our intercessors with God”; the claim illustrates the imagined attachment that the section says disappears at judgment.
None possess ٱلشَّفَٰعَة except one who has a covenant with the Merciful, qualifying rather than erasing the section’s image of unavailable support.
The condemned say فَمَا لَنَا مِن شَٰفِعِينَ, naming their lack of anyone able to join their cause.
Their alleged partners cease to be شُفَعَاء, so supposed association becomes disassociation at the resurrection.
The denial of any protector or شَفِيع besides God places all effective attachment and advocacy under the unmatched Creator.
Intercession does not benefit with God except for one He permits; the ayah marks the controlled exception to judgment-day aloneness.
The believer rejects gods whose شَفَاعَة could not benefit or rescue him if the Merciful intended harm, testing supposed support by its actual power.
The question challenges people for taking شُفَعَاء besides God even when those figures possess and understand nothing, exposing invented companions in one’s cause.
لِّلَّهِ ٱلشَّفَٰعَةُ جَمِيعًا locates every effective intercession with God, explaining why no added person can rival His judgment.
On the approaching day wrongdoers have neither devoted friend nor obeyed شَفِيع, combining emotional companionship and formal advocacy in their absence.
Those invoked besides God do not possess intercession, apart from the truth-bearing witness who knows; the exception defines legitimate advocacy.
فَمَا تَنفَعُهُمْ شَفَٰعَةُ ٱلشَّٰفِعِينَ explicitly makes even existing intercessors’ advocacy useless to the condemned, as the section states.
أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًا فَـَٔاوَىٰ answers orphaned singularity with God-given shelter, providing the positive model for standing beside the orphan.
فَأَمَّا ٱلْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ turns remembered shelter into a direct prohibition against overpowering the unprotected orphan.
True righteousness gives cherished wealth to the orphan among named vulnerable recipients; honoring the solitary child becomes a concrete expenditure rather than praise of uniqueness.
Returning orphans’ property intact protects those who lack a father’s defender and specifies one material form of joining them in support.
When orphans attend an estate division, the ayah commands provision and kind speech for them, bringing those easily excluded into the distribution.
The ruling demands justice for orphan women and vulnerable children, extending “honor the orphan” to those whose isolation exposes them to withheld rights.
God preserves a treasure beneath the wall for two orphan boys until maturity because their father was righteous; divine care supplies the protection their absent father cannot.
The righteous feed an orphan, alongside the needy and captive, despite loving the food; practical care attaches the unprotected person to a giving community.
Feeding يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ on a day of hunger makes kinship with an orphan a demanding path of moral ascent.
Joseph asks تَوَفَّنِى مُسْلِمًا وَأَلْحِقْنِى بِٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ; death is imagined as attachment to the righteous rather than isolated status.
Abraham’s prayer وَأَلْحِقْنِى بِٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ makes being joined to a worthy community a divine gift.
God promises believers لَنُدْخِلَنَّهُمْ فِى ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ, closely matching the section’s admission of one faithful soul into a collective.
Obedience places a person مَعَ ٱلَّذِينَ blessed by God—prophets, truthful, martyrs, and righteous—then calls them excellent companions.
Those who feared their Lord are led to the Garden زُمَرًا; the plural companies give a collective counterpart to the single soul’s command to enter.
Taking God, His messenger, and believers as allies identifies one with حِزْبَ ٱللَّهِ; belonging to God’s party is formed through loyal attachment.
سُبْحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ ٱلْأَزْوَٰجَ كُلَّهَا extends pairing across plants, humans, and unknown creatures, while glorification belongs to their Creator.
God makes زَوْجَيْنِ ٱثْنَيْنِ from every fruit, presenting visible created pairs as signs for reflection.
God creates ٱلزَّوْجَيْنِ ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ, defining the pair through male and female and assigning its making to Him.
From the fashioned human drop God makes ٱلزَّوْجَيْنِ ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ, so paired life arises from a single small origin.
وَخَلَقْنَٰكُمْ أَزْوَٰجًا states human pairing as a direct act of creation.
The oath by the creation of male and female parallels the oath by even and odd, giving the section’s numerical pair a bodily created form.
God creates humanity from نَّفْسٍ وَٰحِدَةٍ and makes from it its mate for repose; the single is not left alone but becomes relational.
One soul, its mate, and eight livestock pairs are placed in one creation account, making singular origin and manifold pairing belong to the one God.
Mates made from yourselves bring repose, affection, and mercy; the ayah explains pairing as the opposite of abandonment rather than mere arithmetic.
Creation as male and female expands into peoples and tribes لِتَعَارَفُوا۟; a pair distinction becomes a network of mutual recognition.
لَا تَتَّخِذُوٓا۟ إِلَٰهَيْنِ ٱثْنَيْنِ ... إِنَّمَا هُوَ إِلَٰهٌ وَٰحِدٌ makes “two” and “one” the grammar of rejecting any divine counterpart.
Joseph contrasts scattered many lords with ٱللَّهُ ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ, turning numerical unity into exclusive sovereignty.
هَلْ تَعْلَمُ لَهُۥ سَمِيًّا asks whether any namesake or peer is known for God, restating incomparability without the section’s word مِثْل.
The Creator of heavens and earth cannot have a child when He has no consort; divine creativity is explicitly separated from creaturely pairing and generation.
God has neither child, partner in rule, nor protector from weakness; the command to magnify Him follows this threefold denial of any needed counterpart.
Had there been multiple gods, each would have taken its creation and risen over the others; the counterfactual makes undivided divine rule incompatible with peers.
The ayah denies God a son and closes with ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ, distinguishing His oneness from all creaturely descent and selection.
The jinn exalt their Lord’s majesty because He has taken neither consort nor child, again placing generative pairing outside divine uniqueness.
أَفَمَن يَخْلُقُ كَمَن لَّا يَخْلُقُ denies likeness between the Creator and non-creators, clarifying why a uniquely made thing cannot share its Maker’s kind of uniqueness.
When God manifests to the mountain He makes it دَكًّا; this concrete crushing supplies the singular prototype for the section’s repeated دَكًّا دَكًّا.
At the promised time God makes the barrier دَكَّآءَ, another divine leveling that lets the section’s repeated crushing be heard as successive instances of His act.
An oath is sworn by those ranged صَفًّا; it parallels the section’s oath-form opening and its later multiplication of rank after rank.
The angels say وَإِنَّا لَنَحْنُ ٱلصَّآفُّونَ, identifying the heavenly beings whose ranked presence forms the judgment scene developed in the section.
The Spirit and angels stand صَفًّا and speak only by the Merciful’s permission; angelic rank and restricted advocacy meet in one last-day scene.
People are presented before their Lord صَفًّا and reminded that they came as first created, combining the judgment rank with stripped, original individuality.
Those who fight in God’s way صَفًّا are likened to a compact structure; a row becomes the visible form of persons joined so none stands unsupported.
The command “seize him and shackle him” begins a divine binding sequence; 69:31-32 names the fire and the immense chain that complete the unmatched punishment scene.
This ayah places the seized person in Hell between the shackling command of 69:30 and chaining of 69:32, identifying the setting and purpose of the bonds.
فِى سِلْسِلَةٍ ... فَٱسْلُكُوهُ gives the binding a seventy-cubit chain, concretizing the divine وثاق whose like the section denies to anyone else.
The criminals are مُقَرَّنِينَ فِى ٱلْأَصْفَادِ—fastened together in fetters; enforced pairing becomes punishment rather than supportive companionship.
أَنكَالًا وَجَحِيمًا promises shackles and a blaze with God, supplying another direct scene of His eschatological binding.
Chains, iron collars, and a blaze are prepared for rejecters, detailing the forms taken by divine restraint.
فَذَٰلِكَ ٱلَّذِى يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ is the exact moral reversal of honoring and joining the orphan: the denier violently drives the solitary child away.
Even if the believers are pleased with the excuse-makers, God is not pleased with the defiantly disobedient; human رضى here fails to become the reciprocal رضى of the section.
Satan takes possession of them and they become حِزْبُ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنِ; it is the opposing community to the divine party into which the faithful soul is admitted.
Earth and mountains are crushed دَكَّةً وَٰحِدَةً, a “single crushing” that illuminates by contrast the section’s paired repetition דَكًّا دَكًّا.
When the trumpet is blown there are no kinship ties and no mutual asking; created relations that normally pair and group people no longer carry them through judgment.
No parent can avail a child and no child a parent on the promised day, marking the boundary where even the closest created pair cannot stand in for the other.
No protective ally avails another at all that day, reversing the section’s social ideal of joining someone as supporter.
No soul possesses anything for another soul and command belongs wholly to God; repeated نَفْسٌ لِّنَفْسٍ pairs the words while denying effective mutual aid.
A person flees from his brother, beginning a family-by-family dissolution of companionship at resurrection that continues through 80:37.
Mother and father are the next relations fled from, showing that the judgment-day singleton is detached even from the pair that produced him.
A spouse and children are also fled from, undoing the household pair and its descendants in the same scene.
Each person has a concern sufficient for him, explaining the solitary self-absorption behind the flights listed in 80:34-36.
No close friend asks about a close friend, so intimate companionship ceases to function in the judgment scene.
Though former intimates are made visible to one another, the guilty person would ransom himself with his children; visibility without solidarity completes 70:10’s failed companionship.
Close friends become enemies that day except the God-conscious; this boundary prepares the enduring servant-community addressed in 43:68-70.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly consume fire into themselves, turning failure to protect the solitary child into an explicitly solitary punishment.
Humans may tighten prisoners’ bonds in war, but the same ayah requires later release or ransom; this temporary, regulated bond marks the boundary from God’s incomparable final binding.
The challenge to produce a surah مِن مِّثْلِهِ and call supporting witnesses tests a claimed likeness through collective help, echoing the section’s link between counterpart and added supporter.
Those alleging invention are told to bring a surah like it and call whomever they can; the failure of assembled helpers establishes an unmatched object.
The challenge asks for ten fabricated surahs مِثْلِهِ and every available helper, again measuring likeness against the strongest possible human association.
Let them bring a discourse مِثْلِهِ if truthful: a proposed counterpart becomes the test of a uniqueness claim.
Solomon asks for a kingdom not fitting anyone after him; its deliberately unrepeatable created distinction remains a granted possession, refining Irem’s boast in being unmatched.
ٱللَّهُ ٱلصَّمَدُ names the One on whom all depend, explaining why His oneness is not the loneliness or need of a created singleton.
He neither begets nor is begotten, excluding the generational relations by which created beings form pairs and lines of descent; it completes 112:1 and 112:4’s incomparable oneness.
إِلَٰهٌ وَٰحِدٌ declares the worshipped God one and immediately names His mercy, placing divine unity in the stance of dependence and worship.

The messenger is بَشَرٌ مِّثْلُكُمْ while the revealed God is إِلَٰهٌ وَٰحِدٌ, and worship must associate no أَحَدًا with Him; human likeness, categorical exclusion, and divine unity are assigned to different levels.
“I am only a human like you” is paired with revelation that your God is one, again distinguishing creaturely similitude from the Creator’s unity.
If heavens and earth contained gods besides God, both would be ruined; cosmic order becomes evidence against divine plurality.
إِنَّ إِلَٰهَكُمْ لَوَٰحِدٌ makes divine oneness the proposition of an oath passage, resonating with the section’s oath by pair and single.
The messenger is told to announce that there is no god but ٱللَّهُ ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ, giving exclusive divine unity a public speaker and addressee.
At universal emergence God asks who owns sovereignty and answers: ٱلْوَٰحِدِ ٱلْقَهَّارِ; solitary human exposure is set before singular divine rule.
All emerge before ٱللَّهِ ٱلْوَٰحِدِ ٱلْقَهَّارِ after earth and heavens are changed, joining the last-day scene to the One before whom each comes.
The prohibition فَلَا تَضْرِبُوا۟ لِلَّهِ ٱلْأَمْثَالَ blocks invented comparisons for God, supporting the section’s move from lexical “counterpart” to divine incomparability.
فَلَا تَجْعَلُوا۟ لِلَّهِ أَندَادًا forbids setting up equals for the Creator who provides earth, sky, and fruit; provision does not make the Giver one member of a pair.
God does not share His rule with أَحَدًا, using the source section’s negative indefinite to make the exclusion comprehensive in sovereignty.
The messenger says he calls on his Lord and associates with Him no أَحَدًا, using categorical negation to enact exclusive worship.
Creation from dust and a drop is followed by ثُمَّ جَعَلَكُمْ أَزْوَٰجًا; the movement from small single origin to pairs depends on God’s knowledge.
God makes spouses from yourselves and from spouses children and grandchildren, showing how a pair opens into the larger human company.
The One who خَلَقَ ٱلْأَزْوَٰجَ كُلَّهَا also provides ships and cattle for riding; paired creation is integrated into human provision.
Sheep and goats are counted as four of ثَمَٰنِيَةَ أَزْوَٰجٍ, making the pair a repeated unit in a larger created total.
Camels and cattle complete the eight pairs begun in 6:143, while the challenge over male and female exposes invented prohibitions imposed on those pairs.
The flood command places مِن كُلٍّ زَوْجَيْنِ ٱثْنَيْنِ in the Ark; paired creatures are preserved together through destruction.
The repeated Ark instruction carries two of every pair, again making companionship the form by which creaturely kinds survive the flood.
God originates the addressed human multitude from نَّفْسٍ وَٰحِدَةٍ, letting plurality retain the trace of a single beginning even without naming the mate here.
The covenant pairs worship of God with kindness to parents, kin, orphans, and the needy; the orphan is placed inside an ordered network of obligations.
Orphans are named among the proper recipients of whatever good wealth is spent, assigning the community a continuing material duty toward them.
Testing orphans to maturity and then delivering their property supplies a patient, accountable form of guardianship until they can stand independently.
Doing good to the orphan appears within a long map of near and distant relations, locating the one without a father inside communal neighborliness.
The orphan’s property may be approached only in the best manner until maturity, placing a protective boundary around the child’s vulnerability.
A fixed share of spoils is assigned to orphans, preventing those without a powerful household defender from being omitted from communal wealth.
The orphan’s property is protected until maturity and covenants must be fulfilled, making support a binding responsibility rather than sentiment.
Orphans receive a share of restored property so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, connecting their inclusion to the shape of the whole economy.
The boastful person loses the wealth and children he claims and comes to God فَرْدًا; earthly additions cannot prevent final singularity.
Everyone in heavens and earth comes to the Merciful as a servant; 19:94 counts them and 19:95 makes each arrival individual.
God has enumerated them exactly, converting the universal servant-company of 19:93 into distinct counted persons before 19:95 says each comes alone.
Worldly bonds formed around idols become mutual denial and cursing at resurrection; a false community dissolves when its members most need support.

Failure to urge feeding the needy precedes the declaration in 69:35 that the condemned person has no devoted friend, giving textual support to the section’s moral link between withheld care and later aloneness.
فَلَيْسَ لَهُ ٱلْيَوْمَ هَٰهُنَا حَمِيمٌ makes the one who did not promote feeding in 69:34 friendless on that day.
The one who drives away the orphan also fails to urge feeding the poor, showing neglect as a paired social pattern rather than an isolated offense.
God is pleased with the believers under the tree; this supplies the divine-to-human side of the reciprocal رضى that the section expresses in paired form.
God does not approve disbelief for His servants but approves gratitude for them, specifying what divine pleasure toward the servant does and does not embrace.
The self-purifying giver who seeks only his Lord’s face “will surely be pleased,” linking human رضى to prior selfless giving.
The Lord’s future gift will make the addressee pleased, presenting divine giving as the cause of the servant’s رضى even though reciprocity is not stated here.
God admits the emigrants and slain into an entrance with which they will be pleased, combining admission with human satisfaction in an afterlife setting.
The Book is مُتَشَٰبِهًا مَّثَانِىَ—internally resembling and recurrent—so likeness and repetition become a textual form analogous to the section’s doubled units.
لَتَرْكَبُنَّ طَبَقًا عَن طَبَقٍ describes passage from stage to stage; succession, rather than a static count, makes one comparable unit follow another.
The rejecters are thrown into a narrow place مُقَرَّنِينَ, where being bound together is a punitive parody of the supportive joining developed in the section.
Solomon has other rebellious beings مُقَرَّنِينَ فِى ٱلْأَصْفَادِ; creaturely delegated binding provides a bounded contrast to the final binding whose equal 89:26 denies.
Collars on necks and chains by which the condemned are dragged render divine restraint as an enacted judgment scene.
Shackles reaching the chins picture rejecters immobilized even before the final day, offering a present moral image of the binding later made unsurpassable.
